title: A Language-Informed Loss for Visual Generation

paper.title: A Language-Informed Loss for Visual Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract End-to-end visual generation with pixel-space loss has recently achieved competitive performance without the need for learned image tokenizers. In this work, we study whether language-informed supervision can provide a richer training signal than pixel loss for visual generation. We introduce LILIE (pronounced “lily”), a L anguage- I nformed and L ossless I mage E ncoder. LILIE is an invertible image transform trained such that a vision-language model can recover captions from noised features. The encoder uses a normalizing flow transformer trained jointly with a vision-language model via next token prediction. We then use the encoder to extract a simple language-informed loss for text-to-image generation. We train JiT models with LILIE loss, reducing gFD by 14 points (66.84 → \to 53.01) against a pixel-only baseline on the GPIC dataset. Our code, encoders, and generative models are available at suchiragarwal.com/lilie .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Image generators are typically built in two stages. A tokenizer first compresses images into a learned latent space, and a generative model is then trained in that space. Latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , autoregressive ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , and mixed-modal ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) generators all follow this recipe. By reducing the dimensionality of the modeling problem, tokenization makes generation more tractable and lowers computational cost. However, the lossy tokenizer bounds achievable quality, particularly for fine-grained content (e.g. rendered text and human faces) ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Recent work removes the first stage entirely. JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) trains a plain transformer end-to-end on raw pixels and achieves competitive performance with two-stage systems without training a tokenizer at all. Pixels are hence an appealing output space, but we ask whether generation quality can be improved by extracting a richer training signal. Figure 2: Two perturbed image patches (additive Gaussian noise) with equal pixel Euclidean distance of 1000 from the original patches. Caption: “Three airplanes fly in the sky against a cloudy backdrop.” Pixel loss measures squared Euclidean distance between predicted and target pixels. However, errors of equal pixel distance can vary in underlying semantic content. Figure 2 shows two perturbations, each with pixel distance of 1000 from the original patches. One perturbation degrades a subject while the other alters a background cloud, but pixel loss treats them the same. We hypothesize that language may help address this gap. Prior work suggests that language provides an inherently semantic signal ( Hockett, 1960 ; Mikolov et al., 2013 ; Barbieri, 2020 ) . Motivated by the semantic gap between language and vision ( Smeulders et al., 2000 ; Collell and Moens, 2016 ) , we study whether distances in a visual space shaped by language can provide a richer training signal to supervise end-to-end visual generation than pixel loss alone. Figure 3: Training and using LILIE. (a) We jointly train LILIE and VLM LoRA parameters on noise-corrupted features with next token prediction. (b) The diffusion model trains on Pixel and LILIE L 2 L^{2} losses, comparing its prediction with the target image in pixel space and through the learned encoder. We introduce LILIE, a Language-Informed and Lossless Image Encoder. LILIE is an invertible transform from ℝ H × W × 3 → ℝ H × W × 3 \mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}\to\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} , trained such that a vision-language model can caption the output after it is corrupted by Gaussian noise. We build LILIE on a transformer normalizing flow architecture ( Zhai et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026b ) , keeping the invertible architecture but replacing the generation objective with a captioning objective. Our method is trained with next token prediction over ground-truth image captions. The encoder learns to arrange its output so that caption-relevant visual information survives the corruption, while invertibility guarantees that no visual information is lost. After training, we discard the VLM and keep LILIE as a simple standalone image transform. We finally train a family of JiT-T2I ( Li and He, 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) models on GPIC ( Chandrasegaran et al., 2026 ) , a large scale open dataset for text-to-image generation. We first pretrain pixel-space and perceptual loss baselines to provide references on the GPIC corpus. We then study the impact of our training signal with LILIE on generation quality by performing comprehensive ablations. We freeze the encoder, apply it to the predicted and target images, and add squared error in LILIE-space to the standard pixel-space flow-matching loss ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) . For our 1.1B parameter JiT-T2I-g, the pixel-only baseline reaches a gFD-DINOv2 ( Stein et al., 2023 ) of 66.84 on the GPIC test set. Replacing the pixel loss entirely with LILIE loss improves this to 55.78, so language supervision alone is already enough to learn a feature space that improves pixel generation. Combining LILIE and pixel losses further improves gFD to 53.01. To summarize, we propose a language-informed loss that improves pixel-space visual generation quality, and we hope our work encourages the community to adopt language-informed losses for training visual generative models. We highlight our main contributions below. • We pretrain language-informed and lossless image encoders. • We pretrain generative models with perceptual losses (LPIPS, DINOv2, SigLIP 2) on the GPIC corpus to provide baseline references. • We pretrain generative models with supervision in LILIE-space and achieve a 14-point reduction in gFD over a pixel-only baseline.

sections.heading: Pixel-space diffusion.
sections.text: Pixel-space diffusion generates images without a learned image tokenizer. Cascaded diffusion models, including Imagen, generate images at progressively higher resolutions ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ) , while Simple diffusion and Recurrent Interface Networks support high-resolution generation without cascades ( Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ; Jabri et al., 2023 ) . More recent approaches include cascaded flow matching in PixelFlow ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , neural field prediction within image patches in PixNerd ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , and joint patch-level and pixel-level processing in PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . JiT predicts clean images directly from noisy pixels ( Li and He, 2026 ) . Pixel MeanFlow extends clean-image prediction to one-step generation with a MeanFlow objective ( Lu et al., 2026a ; Geng et al., 2025 ) . We build on JiT, studying the training loss while keeping the generator architecture fixed.

sections.heading: Feature-space losses for generation.
sections.text: Perceptual losses compare images through neural features, providing supervision beyond pixel-wise error ( Johnson et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2018 ) . PixelGen applies this approach by augmenting a pixel-space flow-matching loss with LPIPS and DINOv2 losses ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . REPA instead aligns the denoiser’s hidden states with features from a pretrained visual encoder ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . PixelREPA finds that directly applying this alignment to JiT can reduce sample quality and diversity, and introduces a masked adapter that improves generation ( Shin et al., 2026 ) . VA-VAE and representation autoencoders also use pretrained visual features to construct latent spaces for diffusion ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . In this work, we learn a language-supervised and lossless representation for the loss while keeping generation in pixel space.

sections.heading: Invertible networks.
sections.text: Prior normalizing flow models such as Real NVP and Glow learn invertible transformations that enable exact likelihood evaluation and sampling ( Dinh et al., 2017 ; Kingma and Dhariwal, 2018 ) . TARFlow extends this approach with autoregressive transformers operating on image patches ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) . Invertible architectures have also been used for representation learning as in i-RevNet ( Jacobsen et al., 2018 ) . IB-INN uses small input perturbations to form an information-bottleneck objective for invertible generative classifiers ( Ardizzone et al., 2020 ) . LILIE uses the improved TARFlow architecture introduced in BiFlow ( Lu et al., 2026b ) . We train this bijection through caption prediction from corrupted features and use its learned feature space to measure errors when training a T2I generator.

sections.heading: Language-supervised visual representations.
sections.text: CLIP learns transferable visual features through contrastive image-text supervision ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , while SigLIP 2 combines image-text alignment with captioning and self-supervised objectives ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) . VirTex and CapPa demonstrate that caption prediction itself can learn effective visual representations ( Desai and Johnson, 2021 ; Tschannen et al., 2023 ) . Language has also been used to inform image tokenization. QLIP and UniTok combine reconstruction and image-text alignment objectives to learn discrete representations ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . TexTok conditions image encoding and decoding on captions, improving reconstruction and downstream generation quality ( Zha et al., 2025 ) . LILIE uses captions as prediction targets for corrupted image features. Caption cross-entropy is our only training loss.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: Pixel-space losses treat errors across pixels equally, even when they differ in relevance to image content. Feature-space losses instead compare images in a feature space that emphasizes certain visual properties. Here, we propose a method for learning such a feature space that is lossless and supervised by language. LILIE learns a bijection ℰ θ : ℝ H × W × 3 → ℝ H × W × 3 \mathcal{E}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}\to\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} from images to equally-shaped features. We train the encoder such that a finetuned VLM can recover an image’s caption from features corrupted with Gaussian noise. This corruption procedure encourages semantic information to remain recoverable under corruption, and invertibility prevents representations from discarding any visual information. Our complete method has two stages. First, we learn an image encoder ℰ θ \mathcal{E}_{\theta} from image-caption pairs. We then freeze the encoder and use L 2 L^{2} in LILIE-space to augment pixel-space loss for training a text-to-image generative model.

sections.heading: Learning an invertible map.
sections.text: We parametrize ℰ θ \mathcal{E}_{\theta} using the improved TARFlow architecture from BiFlow ( Lu et al., 2026b ; Zhai et al., 2025 ) . Unlike prior applications, we do not use this architecture to train a normalizing flow density model. We use it for its invertibility and change the training objective. Figure 4: LILIE training diagram. We expand on Figure 3 (a) to include TARFlow internals. We provide additional details on affine coupling and transformer internals in Appendix A.1 . Figure 4 and Algorithm 1 describe the training procedure to learn ℰ θ \mathcal{E}_{\theta} . Each image is mapped through ℰ θ \mathcal{E}_{\theta} , rescaled to a per-image RMS of 1 / 2 1/2 , corrupted with additive white Gaussian noise, and captioned by a LoRA-finetuned VLM ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . The training signal is cross-entropy of the VLM predictions against the ground-truth GPIC caption. We backpropagate to jointly update ℰ θ \mathcal{E}_{\theta} and the VLM’s LoRA parameters. The RMS target of 1 / 2 1/2 approximately matches the RMS of natural images in the GPIC corpus, keeps LILIE feature scales in-domain for the VLM, and prevents ℰ θ \mathcal{E}_{\theta} from enlarging all features to compensate for the corruption. We also track an EMA estimate of the raw features’ second moment, averaged over all features, which we use for downstream rescaling. sections.heading: Data.
sections.text: All models are trained on the GPIC corpus of image-caption pairs ( Chandrasegaran et al., 2026 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. Following the experimental setup from GPIC, we train both the encoder and diffusion models over one epoch on GPIC Full (100M train examples) at a global batch size of 256, yielding 390,600 steps. Every image in the GPIC corpus is paired with a caption from one of four length classes (tag, short, medium, long), which we match with a corresponding prompt for LILIE training (Appendix F ).

sections.heading: Encoders.
sections.text: Unless otherwise stated, the encoder is LILIE-S, a 32M parameter improved TARFlow ( Lu et al., 2026b ) with K = 4 K=4 blocks, L = 4 L=4 layers per block, bottleneck dimension H = 384 H=384 , and patch size 16. We use SmolVLM-256M ( Marafioti et al., 2025 ) , which we finetune with rank 64 LoRA. We choose SmolVLM-256M as it is a compact openly available VLM, at 8 × 8\times the size of our encoder. Training LILIE-S takes approximately 40 hours on TPU v5e-32. We detail the full configuration in Table B.2 .

sections.heading: Generative models.
sections.text: We train JiT-T2I-XL and -g models ( Li and He, 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) with 700M and 1.1B parameters, respectively. Both condition on a frozen Qwen3-1.7B text encoder ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . We primarily compare three objectives: Pixel, LILIE, and Pixel+LILIE, while holding the generator configuration constant. Our main results train for one epoch on GPIC Full (390,600 steps), and ablations use 200K steps. Training JiT-T2I-XL and -g takes approximately 27 and 40 hours on TPU v6e-16, respectively. We detail the full configurations in Table B.3 .

sections.heading: Perceptual loss baselines.
sections.text: Recent work has shown that perceptual supervision with LPIPS and DINOv2 significantly benefits pixel-space diffusion generation quality ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . These methods follow our general paradigm of combining pixel and feature-space losses, so we pretrain JiT models with perceptual supervision to provide reference baselines. We consider LPIPS with VGG16 ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) and perceptual losses in DINOv2 ViT-B/14 ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) and SigLIP 2 ViT-B/16@256px ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) feature spaces. We pretrain each baseline using a combination of pixel-space loss with a single feature-space loss, and we follow the setup from PixelGen ( Ma et al., 2026 ) while disabling REPA feature alignment. SigLIP 2 provides a language-aligned baseline, and we configure it in an identical manner to P-DINO in PixelGen using cosine dissimilarity. We additionally evaluate each feature space alone, without any pixel-space loss, using L 2 L^{2} distance for DINOv2 and SigLIP 2. We provide full implementation details in Appendix B.2 .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We report Fréchet distance (gFD), precision, recall, density, and coverage (PRDC) ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019 ; Naeem et al., 2020 ) , and squared maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) all in the DINOv2 representation space ( Oquab et al., 2023 ; Stein et al., 2023 ) following the GPIC evaluation protocol. We use generator EMA weights for sampling and select classifier-free guidance (CFG) separately for each model by minimizing gFD on GPIC Validation-50K, then report results on Test-50K. Unless varied below, sampling uses 50 Euler steps.

sections.heading: Hyperparameter selection.
sections.text: We first select the noise level σ \sigma used to train the encoder and loss weight λ \lambda used to train the generator using JiT-T2I-XL at 200K training steps. We compare five noise levels and three mixing weights, as well as the LILIE-only objective. The best setting in this sweep is σ = 0.25 \sigma=0.25 and λ = 2 \lambda=2 , which we use for our main results and ablations. Appendix C details the procedure and full sweep table.

sections.heading: 4.2 Generation Results
sections.text: Figure 5: gFD over prompt length. We take three sets of 50K prompts from GPIC Test, each containing only short, medium, or long captions. We then sample from the Pixel, LILIE, and Pixel+LILIE JiT-T2I-g models at their respective optimal CFG scales (Table B.1 ). We report gFD over the GPIC Test set. Our optimal Pixel+LILIE configuration outperforms the Pixel baseline at every prompt length.

sections.heading: LILIE improves generation quality.
sections.text: Adding LILIE loss to pixel loss improves gFD, precision, recall, coverage, and MMD for both generators (Table 1 ). For JiT-T2I-XL, Pixel+LILIE reduces gFD from 80.24 to 65.86, and for JiT-T2I-g, it reduces gFD from 66.84 to 53.01. Precision and recall improve alongside gFD reduction, so our gain in generation quality results from both higher sample fidelity and better coverage of the real data distribution. We additionally report GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) results in Appendix B.1 . Figure 1 shows samples from JiT-T2I-g trained with Pixel+LILIE loss. Figure 5 provides gFD results when varying prompt length.

sections.heading: LILIE loss can be used on its own.
sections.text: Replacing pixel loss entirely with LILIE loss reduces gFD from 80.24 to 68.88 for JiT-T2I-XL and from 66.84 to 55.78 for JiT-T2I-g. In contrast, we find that perceptual loss baselines fail when used without a pixel loss term (Table 1 ). Since LILIE is a bijection, matching the target image in LILIE-space exactly recovers the target in pixel space, and LILIE-space alone provides a richer training signal than pixels. LILIE therefore provides a useful training objective even without a pixel loss term, while combining the two yields the best generation quality. Figure 6: Effect of informative captions. gFD on GPIC Test-50K for JiT-T2I-XL with Pixel or Pixel+LILIE loss. “Random” indicates replacing ground-truth captions with random token sequences during LILIE training. We observe that this prevents LILIE from learning a representation that improves generation quality.

sections.heading: Language supervision matters.
sections.text: To isolate the role of informative captions, we train a LILIE-S encoder with captions comprising random token sequences. We replace each token in a real caption by an independent uniform draw from the SmolVLM-256M vocabulary, subset to tokens appearing in GPIC Full. We preserve caption lengths and VLM prompts and only randomize the encoder’s training target. The downstream generator still receives the original image-caption pairs. We then train JiT-T2I-XL with Pixel+LILIE loss using this encoder, using the same generator configuration as before. Figure 6 compares this result with Pixel and Pixel+LILIE trained using real captions. With random captions, gFD is 82.06, compared with 80.24 for Pixel and 65.86 for real captions. Hence, the encoder trained on random token captions fails to improve generation quality relative to the pixel-only model, indicating that real captions play a crucial role during LILIE training.

sections.heading: 4.3 Sampling Steps
sections.text: We next vary the number of Euler steps over 10 , 15 , 20 , 25 , 50 , 75 10,15,20,25,50,75 (Figure 7 ). The curves and examples compare JiT-T2I-g models trained to 390,600 steps. Both Pixel and Pixel+LILIE benefit from increasing the budget from 10 to 75 steps. Pixel+LILIE has lower gFD than Pixel at every tested sampling budget. At 25 steps, Pixel+LILIE reaches a gFD of 58.23, already below Pixel with 50 steps at 68.67. The learned loss can therefore improve the tradeoff between generation quality and the number of sampling steps. Beyond 50 steps, the gains are small. Moving to 75 steps reduces gFD from 68.67 to 68.29 for Pixel and from 52.73 to 52.65 for Pixel+LILIE. LILIE sees an increase in gFD from 55.78 to 56.63 from 50 to 75 steps. We retain 50 Euler steps to compare all methods as both Pixel and Pixel+LILIE see minimal gains from moving to 75 steps, and our choice is consistent with JiT-T2I sampling in GPIC ( Chandrasegaran et al., 2026 ) . sections.heading: Model size.
sections.text: We train LILIE- μ \mu (micro), LILIE-T (tiny), and LILIE-S (small) encoders containing 1.5M, 9.1M, and 32M parameters, respectively. All encoders are trained for 1 epoch on GPIC Full (100M image-caption pairs). Increasing encoder size improves gFD for both generators. For JiT-T2I-g, gFD decreases from 84.66 with LILIE- μ \mu to 80.87 with LILIE-T and 76.59 with LILIE-S. Even LILIE- μ \mu improves over the Pixel baseline of 101.66, so a 1.5M parameter encoder already provides a strong training signal. We detail the model configurations in Table B.2 .

sections.heading: Training data.
sections.text: With the LILIE-S architecture fixed, increasing LILIE training from 10M to 30M and 100M images reduces gFD from 97.79 to 93.52 to 91.79, respectively, for JiT-T2I-XL. For g, the same budgets reduce gFD from 83.01 to 81.18 and 76.59. Hence, increasing the encoder’s data and training budget improves generation quality without increasing the generator’s own training budget.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: Figure 9: LILIE provides a stronger training signal closer to the data distribution. Average standard deviation ratios for LILIE versus pixel values x t x_{t} , and residuals from clean images x x , using the LILIE-S encoder on GPIC Nano (1M train images). x t x_{t} denotes linear interpolation between pure noise ( t = 0 t=0 ) and real data ( t = 1 t=1 ) . We have shown that language supervision alone is sufficient to learn a feature space that improves downstream generation quality. Pixel-space losses measure differences without regard to image content. LILIE instead learns its representation through language supervision. Information needed to describe an image must survive corruption, while invertibility guarantees that no visual information is lost. Figure 9 illustrates an important property of the proposed language-informed loss. Near real data, at t = 0.99 t=0.99 , the learned representation amplifies residual standard deviation by approximately 4.9 × 4.9\times relative to pixels despite near-equal scale between raw pixel values and LILIE features. Hence LILIE makes these small deviations more prominent in the supervision and provides a stronger training signal closer to the data distribution, whereas pixel differences provide a comparatively weak signal.

sections.heading: Comparisons with pretrained perceptual losses.
sections.text: We provide results in Table 1 , and Table 4 summarizes the feature space we compare. LILIE-only loss improves generation quality over Pixel by 11 gFD points ( 66.84 → 55.78 66.84\to 55.78 ), while DINOv2, SigLIP 2, and LPIPS losses result in degenerate quality when used without a Pixel loss term. When combined with Pixel loss, LILIE-loss achieves comparable quality to perceptual loss baselines. We recognize that prior work has had success in combining multiple feature-space losses to supervise visual generation ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and we leave experiments of combining Pixel, LILIE, and perceptual supervision to future work. We discuss limitations of our work in Appendix E . sections.heading: A simple language-informed loss for visual generation.
sections.text: In this work, we propose a simple language-informed loss for visual generation, which uses a small 32M parameter invertible encoder for improving end-to-end visual generation. With LILIE, we improve JiT-T2I-g gFD from 66.84 to 55.78, while combining the losses reaches 53.01 (Table 1 ). Our code, encoders, and generative models are available at suchiragarwal.com/lilie .

sections.heading: preprocess in Algorithm 1 .
sections.text: Each GPIC image is resized so that its shorter side is 256 pixels using bicubic interpolation with antialiasing, then center cropped to 256 × 256 256\times 256 . Pixel values p ∈ [ 0,255 ] {p\in[0,255]} are mapped to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] as 2 ​ p / 255 − 1 2p/255-1 .

sections.heading: SmolVLM input.
sections.text: The noisy features are passed to SmolVLM-256M in place of an image. We do not clamp them to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , allowing values outside the usual image range. Since the VLM is finetuned with LoRA during LILIE training, it adapts to these previously out-of-domain input values.

sections.heading: A.1 Encoder Architecture
sections.text: Figure A.1 expands the encoder in Figure 4 . Each image is split into T T patches of dimension D D . The encoder applies K K autoregressive affine blocks, alternating the patch order used by successive blocks, and reassembles the outputs into an image-shaped feature tensor.

sections.heading: Block parameters.
sections.text: For patch t t , the coupling parameters ( α t , μ t ) (\alpha_{t},\mu_{t}) are log-scale and shift vectors. They depend only on patches preceding position t t in the block’s order. Both vectors are clipped to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] before applying the affine map shown in Figure A.1 (a). The first patch passes through unchanged.

sections.heading: Transformer internals.
sections.text: Each block projects patch vectors from D D dimensions to bottleneck dimension H H , adds learned positional embeddings, and applies L L causal transformer layers. Each layer uses H / 64 H/64 attention heads and an MLP with expansion ratio four and GELU activation, with residual connections around attention and the MLP. Attention uses layer normalization. The final zero-initialized linear head produces 2 ​ D 2D values per position. We drop the last position, prepend zeros, and clip the result. This shift makes each patch’s parameters depend only on earlier patches. The model-size ablation varies K K , H H , and L L , and the configurations are detailed in Table B.2 . The tuple γ t = ( α t , μ t ) \gamma_{t}=(\alpha_{t},\mu_{t}) contains the log-scale and shift of patch t t . (b) The causal transformer within one block, with bottleneck dimension H H and L L layers. LN denotes layer normalization. The lower row expands one transformer layer.

sections.heading: Appendix E Limitations
sections.text: We perform all of our experiments on a single corpus, resolution, and generator family, namely GPIC at 256 × 256 256\times 256 with JiT-T2I. Additionally, training the encoder requires captions and a VLM, and we study only the SmolVLM-256M backbone. A larger VLM may help construct a better feature space, but it comes at an increase in encoder training cost. For LILIE training, we follow the GPIC setup of training our encoder for one epoch on GPIC Full, but we do not propose a method of determining the optimal training budget. Our largest version of LILIE is a 32M parameter encoder, and we do not experiment on scales closer to DINOv2 and SigLIP 2 base model sizes (86M parameters). We do not experiment with combinations of LILIE and perceptual losses.

In this work, we study whether language-informed supervision can provide a richer training signal than pixel loss for visual generation. We introduce LILIE (pronounced “lily”), a L anguage- I nformed and L ossless I mage E ncoder. LILIE is an invertible image transform trained such that a vision-language model can recover captions from noised features. The encoder uses a normalizing flow transformer trained jointly with a vision-language model via next token prediction. We then use the encoder to extract a simple language-informed loss for text-to-image generation. We train JiT models with LILIE loss, reducing gFD by 14 points (66.84 → \to 53.01) against a pixel-only baseline on the GPIC dataset. Our code, encoders, and generative models are available at suchiragarwal.com/lilie . † † footnotetext: Correspondence to suchir@cs.stanford.edu . Figure 1: Generation quality with LILIE. Upper left: Pixel and LILIE supervision at two generator sizes evaluated on GPIC Test-50K with 50 Euler steps. CFG scale is selected using GPIC Validation-50K. All models are trained for one epoch on GPIC Full ( Chandrasegaran et al., 2026 ) . Mosaic: selected × 256 256\!\times\!256 samples from the 1.1B diffusion model with LILIE supervision. Four samples include prompt excerpts. We include randomly selected samples from GPIC Test-50K in Appendix G . 1 Introduction Image generators are typically built in two stages. A tokenizer first compresses images into a learned latent space, and a generative model is then trained in that space. Latent diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) , autoregressive ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , and mixed-modal ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) generators all follow this recipe. By reducing the dimensionality of the modeling problem, tokenization makes generation more tractable and lowers computational cost. However, the lossy tokenizer bounds achievable quality, particularly for fine-grained content (e.g. rendered text and human faces) ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Recent work removes the first stage entirely. JiT ( Li and He, 2026 ) trains a plain transformer end-to-end on raw pixels and achieves competitive performance with two-stage systems without training a tokenizer at all. Pixels are hence an appealing output space, but we ask whether generation quality can be improved by extracting a richer training signal. Figure 2: Two perturbed image patches (additive Gaussian noise) with equal pixel Euclidean distance of 1000 from the original patches. Caption: “Three airplanes fly in the sky against a cloudy backdrop.” Pixel loss measures squared Euclidean distance between predicted and target pixels. However, errors of equal pixel distance can vary in underlying semantic content. Figure 2 shows two perturbations, each with pixel distance of 1000 from the original patches. One perturbation degrades a subject while the other alters a background cloud, but pixel loss treats them the same. We hypothesize that language may help address this gap. Prior work suggests that language provides an inherently semantic signal ( Hockett, 1960 ; Mikolov et al., 2013 ; Barbieri, 2020 ) . Motivated by the semantic gap between language and vision ( Smeulders et al., 2000 ; Collell and Moens, 2016 ) , we study whether distances in a visual space shaped by language can provide a richer training signal to supervise end-to-end visual generation than pixel loss alone. Figure 3: Training and using LILIE. (a) We jointly train LILIE and VLM LoRA parameters on noise-corrupted features with next token prediction. (b) The diffusion model trains on Pixel and LILIE L 2 L^{2} losses, comparing its prediction with the target image in pixel space and through the learned encoder. We introduce LILIE, a Language-Informed and Lossless Image Encoder. LILIE is an invertible transform from ℝ H × W × 3 → ℝ H × W × 3 \mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}\to\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} , trained such that a vision-language model can caption the output after it is corrupted by Gaussian noise. We build LILIE on a transformer normalizing flow architecture ( Zhai et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026b ) , keeping the invertible architecture but replacing the generation objective with a captioning objective. Our method is trained with next token prediction over ground-truth image captions. The encoder learns to arrange its output so that caption-relevant visual information survives the corruption, while invertibility guarantees that no visual information is lost. After training, we discard the VLM and keep LILIE as a simple standalone image transform. We finally train a family of JiT-T2I ( Li and He, 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) models on GPIC ( Chandrasegaran et al., 2026 ) , a large scale open dataset for text-to-image generation. We first pretrain pixel-space and perceptual loss baselines to provide references on the GPIC corpus. We then study the impact of our training signal with LILIE on generation quality by performing comprehensive ablations. We freeze the encoder, apply it to the predicted and target images, and add squared error in LILIE-space to the standard pixel-space flow-matching loss ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) . For our 1.1B parameter JiT-T2I-g, the pixel-only baseline reaches a gFD-DINOv2 ( Stein et al., 2023 ) of 66.84 on the GPIC test set. Replacing the pixel loss entirely with LILIE loss improves this to 55.78, so language supervision alone is already enough to learn a feature space that improves pixel generation. Combining LILIE and pixel losses further improves gFD to 53.01. To summarize, we propose a language-informed loss that improves pixel-space visual generation quality, and we hope our work encourages the community to adopt language-informed losses for training visual generative models. We highlight our main contributions below. • We pretrain language-informed and lossless image encoders. • We pretrain generative models with perceptual losses (LPIPS, DINOv2, SigLIP 2) on the GPIC corpus to provide baseline references. • We pretrain generative models with supervision in LILIE-space and achieve a 14-point reduction in gFD over a pixel-only baseline. 2 Related Work Pixel-space diffusion. Pixel-space diffusion generates images without a learned image tokenizer. Cascaded diffusion models, including Imagen, generate images at progressively higher resolutions ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ) , while Simple diffusion and Recurrent Interface Networks support high-resolution generation without cascades ( Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ; Jabri et al., 2023 ) . More recent approaches include cascaded flow matching in PixelFlow ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , neural field prediction within image patches in PixNerd ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , and joint patch-level and pixel-level processing in PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . JiT predicts clean images directly from noisy pixels ( Li and He, 2026 ) . Pixel MeanFlow extends clean-image prediction to one-step generation with a MeanFlow objective ( Lu et al., 2026a ; Geng et al., 2025 ) . We build on JiT, studying the training loss while keeping the generator architecture fixed. Feature-space losses for generation. Perceptual losses compare images through neural features, providing supervision beyond pixel-wise error ( Johnson et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2018 ) . PixelGen applies this approach by augmenting a pixel-space flow-matching loss with LPIPS and DINOv2 losses ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . REPA instead aligns the denoiser’s hidden states with features from a pretrained visual encoder ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . PixelREPA finds that directly applying this alignment to JiT can reduce sample quality and diversity, and introduces a masked adapter that improves generation ( Shin et al., 2026 ) . VA-VAE and representation autoencoders also use pretrained visual features to construct latent spaces for diffusion ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . In this work, we learn a language-supervised and lossless representation for the loss while keeping generation in pixel space. Invertible networks. Prior normalizing flow models such as Real NVP and Glow learn invertible transformations that enable exact likelihood evaluation and sampling ( Dinh et al., 2017 ; Kingma and Dhariwal, 2018 ) . TARFlow extends this approach with autoregressive transformers operating on image patches ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) . Invertible architectures have also been used for representation learning as in i-RevNet ( Jacobsen et al., 2018 ) . IB-INN uses small input perturbations to form an information-bottleneck objective for invertible generative classifiers ( Ardizzone et al., 2020 ) . LILIE uses the improved TARFlow architecture introduced in BiFlow ( Lu et al., 2026b ) . We train this bijection through caption prediction from corrupted features and use its learned feature space to measure errors when training a T2I generator. Language-supervised visual representations. CLIP learns transferable visual features through contrastive image-text supervision ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , while SigLIP 2 combines image-text alignment with captioning and self-supervised objectives ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) . VirTex and CapPa demonstrate that caption prediction itself can learn effective visual representations ( Desai and Johnson, 2021 ; Tschannen et al., 2023 ) . Language has also been used to inform image tokenization. QLIP and UniTok combine reconstruction and image-text alignment objectives to learn discrete representations ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) . TexTok conditions image encoding and decoding on captions, improving reconstruction and downstream generation quality ( Zha et al., 2025 ) . LILIE uses captions as prediction targets for corrupted image features. Caption cross-entropy is our only training loss. 3 Methodology Pixel-space losses treat errors across pixels equally, even when they differ in relevance to image content. Feature-space losses instead compare images in a feature space that emphasizes certain visual properties. Here, we propose a method for learning such a feature space that is lossless and supervised by language. LILIE learns a bijection ℰ θ : ℝ H × W × 3 → ℝ H × W × 3 \mathcal{E}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}\to\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} from images to equally-shaped features. We train the encoder such that a finetuned VLM can recover an image’s caption from features corrupted with Gaussian noise. This corruption procedure encourages semantic information to remain recoverable under corruption, and invertibility prevents representations from discarding any visual information. Our complete method has two stages. First, we learn an image encoder ℰ θ \mathcal{E}_{\theta} from image-caption pairs. We then freeze the encoder and use L 2 L^{2} in LILIE-space to augment pixel-space loss for training a text-to-image generative model. 3.1 LILIE: A Language-Informed and Lossless Image Encoder Learning an invertible map. We parametrize ℰ θ \mathcal{E}_{\theta} using the improved TARFlow architecture from BiFlow ( Lu et al., 2026b ; Zhai et al., 2025 ) . Unlike prior applications, we do not use this architecture to train a normalizing flow density model. We use it for its invertibility and change the training objective. All models are trained on the GPIC corpus of image-caption pairs ( Chandrasegaran et al., 2026 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. Every image in the GPIC corpus is paired with a caption from one of four length classes (tag, short, medium, long), which we match with a corresponding prompt for LILIE training (Appendix F ). Encoders. Unless otherwise stated, the encoder is LILIE-S, a 32M parameter improved TARFlow ( Lu et al., 2026b ) with K = 4 K=4 blocks, L = 4 L=4 layers per block, bottleneck dimension H = 384 H=384 , and patch size 16. Training LILIE-S takes approximately 40 hours on TPU v5e-32. We detail the full configuration in Table B.2 . Generative models. We train JiT-T2I-XL and -g models ( Li and He, 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) with 700M and 1.1B parameters, respectively. Both condition on a frozen Qwen3-1.7B text encoder ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . We primarily compare three objectives: Pixel, LILIE, and Pixel+LILIE, while holding the generator configuration constant. Our main results train for one epoch on GPIC Full (390,600 steps), and ablations use 200K steps. Training JiT-T2I-XL and -g takes approximately 27 and 40 hours on TPU v6e-16, respectively. We detail the full configurations in Table B.3 . Perceptual loss baselines. Recent work has shown that perceptual supervision with LPIPS and DINOv2 significantly benefits pixel-space diffusion generation quality ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . These methods follow our general paradigm of combining pixel and feature-space losses, so we pretrain JiT models with perceptual supervision to provide reference baselines. We have shown that language supervision alone is sufficient to learn a feature space that improves downstream generation quality. Pixel-space losses measure differences without regard to image content. LILIE instead learns its representation through language supervision. Information needed to describe an image must survive corruption, while invertibility guarantees that no visual information is lost. Figure 9 illustrates an important property of the proposed language-informed loss. Near real data, at t = 0.99 t=0.99 , the learned representation amplifies residual standard deviation by approximately 4.9 × 4.9\times relative to pixels despite near-equal scale between raw pixel values and LILIE features. Hence LILIE makes these small deviations more prominent in the supervision and provides a stronger training signal closer to the data distribution, whereas pixel differences provide a comparatively weak signal. Comparisons with pretrained perceptual losses. We provide results in Table 1 , and Table 4 summarizes the feature space we compare. LILIE-only loss improves generation quality over Pixel by 11 gFD points ( 66.84 → 55.78 66.84\to 55.78 ), while DINOv2, SigLIP 2, and LPIPS losses result in degenerate quality when used without a Pixel loss term. When combined with Pixel loss, LILIE-loss achieves comparable quality to perceptual loss baselines. We recognize that prior work has had success in combining multiple feature-space losses to supervise visual generation ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and we leave experiments of combining Pixel, LILIE, and perceptual supervision to future work.
